title: The Day of Pardon (2000)
hookLine: in St Peter's, the pope publicly asks forgiveness for sins committed by Catholics through history

lines: WRONGS DONE BY ITS OWN MEMBERS.
cards: A Sunday in Lent, in St Peter's Basilica, and a crucifix stands near an old pope. One after another, cardinals and bishops step forward, and each names a kind of wrong. Not wrongs done to the Church.
Wrongs done by its own members. After each one there's silence, and then the pope speaks a prayer asking pardon, and the people answer. Before it ends, the pope goes to the crucifix and kisses it.
He was John Paul the Second, frail by then. The Church remembers it as the Day of Pardon: a very old institution, under its own well-known dome, saying out loud, we did this.

teach.b: The prayers came in a set order.

First, what was named: sins committed in the service of truth, divisions among Christians, sins against the people of Israel, wrongs against love, peace and the dignity of peoples and cultures, against women, against the poor and the unborn.
Broad on purpose. Some listeners wanted more names and details; some thought it went too far. Both reactions were real.

teach.h: A HOLY CHURCH, MEMBERS WHO SIN.
teach.b: The Church teaches that the Church itself is holy, and also that its members sin. So the prayers were spoken for the sins of her sons and daughters, past and present.
Theologians had worked on exactly that distinction in a document called Memory and Reconciliation. Third, the scripture underneath.

teach.h: IF WE SAY WE HAVE NO SIN.
teach.b: The first letter of John says it plainly, in the Douay-Rheims: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us."
A Church that says that to each person in confession was saying it about itself. Fourth, the other half.

teach.h: WE FORGIVE, AND WE ASK FORGIVENESS.
teach.b: In his homily that day the pope paired two things: we forgive, and we ask forgiveness. Catholics have an old phrase for owning a wrong, from the Confiteor, one of the prayers that can open Mass: through my fault.

teach.h: THE TRUTH IS NOT IN US.
teach.b: That day a whole Church said it about its own history. It didn't settle everything. An apology spoken in Rome is a beginning.
What comes after it is the hard part, and some of that story comes tomorrow.

how: Catholics confess their own sins in the sacrament of penance and say the Confiteor, with its words through my fault, at the start of Mass; the Day of Pardon brought that language to the Church's own history.

o: a Latin blessing asking God to forgive others
a formal apology a court orders someone to make
through my fault: owning a wrong as your own

games.q: you're planning a Church's apology for its history. how do you frame it?
o: say the Church itself never did wrong, so nothing is owed.
ask pardon for the sins of its members, named in broad kinds, in public prayer.
games.why: the prayers named kinds of wrong, one by one, and asked pardon for the sins of the Church's sons and daughters.

practice: Recall something that went wrong between you and someone else, where the blame is shared. Don't add up their part; find your own piece and name it plainly to yourself, the way those bishops did, in one sentence with no excuses.
If you pray, bring it to God, perhaps with the old words, through my fault; if not, hold it honestly, without punishing yourself.

wordCard.voice: Mea culpa. Through my fault, the old phrase from the Confiteor that the whole Church said about its own history on the Day of Pardon.

orig.note: Latin: through my fault, from the Confiteor said at the start of Mass.

carryVoice: Your line: we ask forgiveness. And in the same breath: we forgive. That's day nine hundred twenty-eight.
